passage:
"Papa, why is the sky blue?" asked Gopika, swinging her legs on the kitchen stool.
"Good question, what do you think?" said Asif, chopping onions.
"Because the sea is blue and it goes up?"
"Interesting idea! Where does the sea go?"
"Into the clouds?"
"And then?"
Gopika giggled. "Rain! Then it comes down. So the sky is the sea's home."
"That's a lovely thought. Let's look at a book tonight and see what it says."
"Okay! Papa, why do onions make you cry?"
"Ah. What do you think?"
Gopika frowned and thought very hard.

qa.q: What was Gopika sitting on when asking about the sky?
qa.a: The kitchen stool.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling while thinking hard about the onions?
qa.a: Curious and absorbed, with the frown showing real thinking.

qa.q: What did Asif do that helped questions lead somewhere?
qa.a: Asif asked "What do you think?" and followed the ideas with more questions, then promised to check a book together.

qa.q: How might Asif have felt about the endless questions?
qa.a: Warm and interested, since Asif kept chopping while inviting each thought and said the idea was lovely.

grounding: A child asks what and why questions, and answers that invite wondering teach that questions lead somewhere.

passage:
Note from Sudha, nursery teacher.
Today Divyansh asked questions all morning. "Why is the ant small? Why does it walk in a line?" At first Divyansh accepted any answer, nodding at whatever I said. So I tried a change. When Divyansh asked why the ants walk in a line, I said, "What do you think?" Divyansh watched them for a long time and said, "Maybe they're holding hands with their feet." Then Divyansh asked, "Who is the leader?" I will keep asking what the children think before I answer, and see what that opens.

qa.q: What did Divyansh ask about the ants?
qa.a: Why they walk in a line.

qa.q: What did Divyansh's long look at the ants suggest about how Divyansh felt?
qa.a: Curious and absorbed. Divyansh was thinking, and came up with an idea and a new question.

qa.q: What did Sudha change, and what came of it?
qa.a: Sudha asked "What do you think?" before answering, and Divyansh came up with a guess and asked a new question about the leader.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel about being asked instead of told?
qa.a: Interested and trusted, since Divyansh offered a guess and was eager to follow the line to the wall.

grounding: A child asks many questions and accepts any answer, and an adult who asks what do you think teaches that questions lead somewhere.

passage: In their Stockholm apartment, Oskar, five, pressed his nose to the frosty window. "Mamma, what is snow made of?" Astrid thought. "What do you think?" Oskar frowned. "Cold rain?" "Yes, a bit like frozen rain." "Why is it white?" "What do you think?" "Because it's cold and cold is white!" Astrid smiled. "Let's look at one flake on your mitten." They went to the balcony. Oskar stared at the tiny star on his mitten. "It has points! Why does it have points?" Astrid laughed. "Let's find out together."

qa.q: What did Oskar look at on his mitten?
qa.a: A tiny snowflake shaped like a star.

qa.q: How did Oskar feel when he saw the snowflake?
qa.a: He felt amazed and curious, asking why it had points.

qa.q: What did Astrid do that kept Oskar wondering?
qa.a: She asked 'What do you think?' and then showed him a real snowflake, so each answer led to more questions.

qa.q: How might Astrid feel during the snow questions?
qa.a: She seems happy and amused, enjoying finding out together.

grounding: Shows a young child asking endless what and why questions, and an adult answering with 'what do you think' so questions lead somewhere.

passage: At the children's library in Indiranagar, Kiran, five, pointed at the spines of the books. "Why do the books have numbers?" Tanvir, the librarian, crouched down. "What do you think?" Kiran thought hard. "So they don't get lost?" "That's a good guess! What else could the numbers do?" "Tell you where to put them?" "Yes! Want to see where the dinosaur books live?" Kiran nodded. They found the number together. Kiran pulled out a dinosaur book and asked, "Why is this one number five-six-seven?" Tanvir grinned. "Let's find out."

qa.q: What did Kiran ask about the books?
qa.a: Why the books have numbers.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel when finding the dinosaur books?
qa.a: Kiran felt excited and curious, asking another question right away.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do that taught Kiran questions lead somewhere?
qa.a: Tanvir asked 'What do you think?' and built on Kiran's guesses, then took Kiran to find the answer together.

qa.q: How might Tanvir enjoy helping Kiran?
qa.a: Tanvir seems pleased and warm, grinning and joining the search.

grounding: Shows a young child asking many what and why questions, and an adult inviting further wondering instead of just answering.

passage:
Monday: Bhavna, five, asked Papa, "Why is the moon round?" Papa, busy, said, "Just like that." Bhavna said, "Okay," and went back to her crayons.
Wednesday: "Papa, why do birds fly?" This time Lokesh put his phone down. "What do you think, Bhavna?" She thought. "Because they have wings?" "Yes! Why do wings help?" "Because they flap!"
Saturday: On the balcony, Bhavna watched a crow. "Papa, why does it hop sometimes and fly sometimes? What do you think?" Lokesh laughed. "Good question. What do YOU think?" They watched the crow together, guessing.

qa.q: What did Papa say on Monday when Bhavna asked about the moon?
qa.a: He said, 'Just like that.'

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel on Saturday watching the crow?
qa.a: She felt curious and excited, asking her own follow-up and guessing with Papa.

qa.q: What changed in how Lokesh answered, and why did it matter?
qa.a: He started asking 'What do you think?', which taught Bhavna that questions lead to more thinking.

qa.q: What changed in Bhavna between Monday and Saturday?
qa.a: On Monday she accepted any answer; by Saturday she was asking Papa what he thought too.

grounding: Shows a young child who accepts any answer learning, through 'what do you think', that questions lead somewhere.

passage: The power went out at dinner. Sumit Mama switched on a torch and stood it on the table. On the wall, Darshan's shadow jumped up huge. "Why am I so big?" "Hmm. What do you think?" Darshan thought. "Because I'm strong?" "Could be. What happens if you move closer to the torch?" Darshan shuffled forward. The shadow grew even bigger. He gasped and ran back to the wall. It shrank. "Why?!" "What do you think the torch is doing?" "...Making it?" They were still making shadow animals when the lights came back, and Darshan groaned.

qa.q: What did Sumit Mama stand on the table?
qa.a: He stood a torch on the table.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel when his shadow grew bigger?
qa.a: He felt amazed and excited 😊 gasping and running back and forth to test it.

qa.q: Why was "What do you think?" a helpful answer?
qa.a: It let Darshan make a guess and test it, so his questions led somewhere instead of stopping at one answer.

qa.q: How might Sumit Mama feel when Darshan groans at the lights coming back?
qa.a: He probably feels amused and pleased that the power cut turned into a game Darshan didn't want to end.

grounding: Shows a young child's stream of what and why questions during a power cut, and an adult answering with invitations to wonder.
